utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we, first of all, take the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Belinda Pidwell, Tom Hannis, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, we observe that your client is not present this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was informed that he filed his waiver due to some religious ceremony which -- due to be held this morning. But, of course, I will -- I will check with the Registry if -- if they properly informed the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand the Registry hasn't yet received the waiver, but we assume it's in process.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I assume too, and I will get back to the Trial Chamber as soon as I check the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. Yes, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, unfortunately, we're unable to start the witness, who is currently scheduled to commence at 9.00, until later on this morning. And we're seeking the Court's indulgence in this regard. He only arrived over the weekend and was scheduled to be proofed by the OTP yesterday. The interpreter called in sick on Sunday morning, and we were unable to find a replacement interpreter during the course of the day. The witness did spend the day listening to his prior testimony, and we anticipate that we only need one hour with him this morning in order to finalise his proofing. He is here, and the lawyer who is leading him is seeing him now. And so we're asking for your indulgence to adjourn and recommence at 11.00 this morning because of those circumstances. We've consulted the Defence on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do counsel for the Defence have any comments or observations on the application by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We don't oppose, Your Honours. We understand the situation, as -- as explained by Ms. Pidwell. There's nothing we can do anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: We do anticipate that we will be finished with this witness today. He is the only witness we have today because of the last-minute changes towards -- at the end of last week when the videolink witness was cancelled. And, accordingly, we only have one hour in chief with him; the Defence have approximately an hour, maybe an hour and a half. So we do anticipate we will be finished with the witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we adjourn, to resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may the record -- [French on English Channel] ... show that Ms. Tatjana Savic joined the Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And what -- [Microphone not activated] ... Mr. Zecevic, the witness who is scheduled to begin this morning, could you alert me as to how much time the Defence has asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We estimated our cross-examination, I believe, one -- one and a -- one session or one hour. I'm not sure at this moment, but I can check, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... I just need an idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... Thank you. And, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Our estimation was in general because this witness is not related to our municipalities; but, if any, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But, to be sure, maybe -- maybe we shouldn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- not have any cross-examination. And, Your Honours, I would like just to inform you that, from UNDU and Registry, a waiver of my client was distributed, so everything is in order now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For the record, is there a change in the appearances for the Prosecution today from what we had at 9.00 this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There is a change. This is Gerard Dobbyn for the Office of the Prosecutor, along with Tom Hannis and Crispian Smith. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please have the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may be seated, sir. I trust that you can hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Would you begin by telling us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Sulejman Crncalo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth, and what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 15th February 1945. I'm an ethnic Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was first a lathe operator. And later, I was a traffic technician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you testified previously before this Tribunal or before any of the courts in the former Yugoslavia in relation to matters arising of what happened there in the late -- in the early 1990s and moving forward?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I testified here before, twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, in that case, I need only remind you of the procedure of the Tribunal, which is -- which it has in common with most courts; that is, that in these proceedings, your testimony would be led by the side calling you - in this case, the Prosecution - who has asked for a total of about an hour and a quarter for their examination-in-chief. And counsel for each of the accused would have a right to cross-examine. Counsel for the accused Mr. Stanisic has indicated they would only spend about an hour. And counsel for the second accused Mr. Zupljanin has indicated that if they cross-examine at all, it would only be about 15 minutes. So, all in all, it is expected that your testimony would be completed before the Tribunal takes its adjournment for the day at 1.45. And the -- our time is a little irregular today, in that we are starting a little later than we thought; but notwithstanding that, as I said, it is still expected that your testimony will be completed. We will take one break between now and 1.45, so your testimony would not be continuous. But if, for any reason, you need to the Tribunal to -- if you need to take a break, you can indicate that and we will accommodate you. And with that, I would invite Mr. Dobbyn to begin his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Crncalo.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, did you testify in the Krajisnik case on the 2nd and 3rd of September, 2004?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Since arriving here in The Hague, have you had an opportunity to listen to that testimony from the Krajisnik case?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: You mean when I came this time? I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Was the recording you listened to an accurate record of your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And is the information that was contained in that testimony in the Krajisnik case the same as you would give if testifying in full today?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like to tender the witness's 92 ter testimony an associated exhibits. And they have 65 ter numbers 10390.01 to 10390.04.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I believe, as is our practice, your application to -- the decision on the application is -- is deferred to the end of the testimony. But your application is noted for the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. At this time, with the Court's leave, I would like to read a very brief summary of his testimony in the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo is a Bosnian Muslim who lived and worked in Pale from 1978 until he was expelled on the 2nd of July, 1992. His 92 ter testimony provides an overview of the persecution and forced transfer of Muslims in Pale in the period from late 1991 until July 1992. The Bosnian Serb forces, including the police, participated in this campaign of persecution and forcible transfer. Throughout this period, Mr. Crncalo and other Muslim representatives held meetings with Serb officials, including the chief of police Malko Koroman, in an effort to ease the conditions under which the non-Serbs in Pale were existing. A member of the Bosnian Serb Presidency, Nikola Koljevic, attended one of these meetings. Rather than addressing their concerns, they were told by Mr. Koljevic that regardless of what they, the Muslims, wanted, the Serbs did not want Muslims living in Pale. Bosnian Serb forces randomly arrested non-Serbs in Pale. Mr. Crncalo himself was arrested, taken to the SJB building, and beaten before being released later the same day. Other Muslims were also arbitrarily detained, and some were killed. Finally, Mr. Crncalo was part of a convoy of non-Serbs expelled from Pale on the 2nd of July, 1992. That concludes the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Crncalo, I'd like to ask you some questions that just clarify and expand on some of the events that you described in your Krajisnik testimony. And, first, I'd like to turn to your detention on the 3rd of March, 1992. And in your prior testimony in Krajisnik you described being arrested by three reserve policemen on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And this is at transcript page 5309 of his 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Crncalo, at the time that you were arrested outside your house, were you told by these reserve policemen why you were being arrested?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: They didn't tell me anything. Two of them, from the sides, squatted on their knees on the ground, trained guns at me, and another one approached me, pushed me into the car, and they took me to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And you described that when you were taken to the police station, you were interrogated by a police inspector named Hrsum. Now, when this police inspector interrogated you, what questions did he ask you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: He asked me where I was going and who had sent me. He asked me the same question several times, and I kept giving the same answer. I wasn't going anywhere. Nobody had sent me. I was just standing outside my house. And as he was asking me the same question, he started beating me; first, slapping and punching. I tried to defend myself by raising my hands to my face. But then he took a truncheon or a wooden club, a bit like a baseball bat, and started beating me with that. And in the meantime, he was calling policemen from the neighbouring room to take me away and kill me. However, nobody came and he continued to beat me. Then he called out to the policemen to take me to Mount Jahorina to kill me. And he called the police five times, but none of them showed up to take me. And ultimately somebody in civilian clothes came, pushed away this thug who was beating me, and told me that I won't be beaten anymore. My pack of cigarettes was on the table. The thug took them, lit one cigarette, and said, Whose cigarettes are these? The first time I didn't answer. The second time I said, They're mine. This man was Hrsum. And he said, Nobody must touch these. Then he -- they took me away. And then the same three policemen who arrested me and handcuffed me came to bring my neighbour this time, Munib Kadiric, into the same room. And in the mean time, Hrsum had forced me to get out into the hallway. Inside remained Munib Kadiric. And I hear from the hallway the tables and chairs were being moved and squeaking. I heard blows. And I can't tell you exactly how long it was before Malko Koroman, the chief of police, came through the door. We knew each other from before. He asked me, What are you doing here? And I said, Ask your policemen. He said, Come inside this room. And he was showing the same room where Hrsum had interrogated and beaten me. I said, I was told not to get in anymore; they just forced me out of there. And Koroman insisted. So I got into that room, and Munib Kadiric and I found ourselves together with Malko Koroman. Malko told me to sit down, and he asked me and my neighbour, Where were you arrested? I said, Outside my house. And Munib said the same. And then he says, motioning to his rifle and our rifles on the table, and he says - using the profanity; I don't want to mention it - he says, If any of my men get killed, I will raze your neighbourhood to the ground. And I tell him, Look, let's find a peaceful way to live side by side like we did before. And we also asked that the police be made mixed again, that the Muslim policemen be I allowed to join the force again to serve together. And he says, Until a Serb policeman gets to serve on the force in Stari Grad, Muslims won't be allowed to serve in Pale. And then he told us to go home. It was around 5.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If I could just ask you a couple of questions about what you've spoken about so far. When you were being beaten by this inspector Hrsum, were your hands free?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No, I was handcuffed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And how long did this beating last?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I was brought to the police station around 10.30 in the evening; in other words, 2230. My neighbour Munib Kadiric could have been brought about three hours later. That means that I was beaten for about three hours, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could you describe what injuries, if any, you suffered, as a result of this beating.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I had internal hemorrhages on the back. My face was bruised and swollen from the blows. That subsided after three days. But there were no lacerations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: When you spoke to Malko Koroman immediately after being beaten, did he ask you about your injuries?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No, he didn't ask me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did he give you any indication that he would investigate what had happened to you in the police station?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: He didn't say a word about the way I looked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And finally on this topic, as a result of this arrest, were you charged with anything by the police?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on now to another topic and that's the disarming of the Muslim population in Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, in the transcript, page 10, 1, it looks like if the witness said that there -- something about Malko Koroman's and our rifles on the table. I don't suppose he was arrested with rifles or that there were -- that there were his rifles on the table. Can you clarify that, that there's no mistake?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no mistake. That's contained in his 92 ter transcript. And as he testifies there, he was arrested while standing guard outside his home where his rifle with leaning against this building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So it was his -- it was their rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: It was his -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, in your Krajisnik testimony, you described Malko Koroman appearing on television and calling for non-Serbs to surrender their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: This is at transcript page 5317.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And I'd like to ask you, Did he explicitly state that it was non-Serbs only who were required to hand in their weapons?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I can see Malko Koroman still in my mind's eye. He was appearing on television that night. And, with tears in his eyes, he was saying, Regrettably, there is a war going on in Pale too, and all non-Serbs must turn in all long-barrelled guns. And that meant the weapons of Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: How were these weapons collected, and who collected them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly how much time we were given, but everyone handed in their weapons at the police station. In other local communes where it was not easy for people to get to the police station, because some neighbourhoods are quite far from the urban part of Pale, the police designated certain places where people from the surrounding local communes should turn in their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I move on, now, to a meeting you described with Malko Koroman and Mr. Koljevic. And you described that you had this meeting to discuss the security of Muslims in Pale. And you testified that Mr. Koljevic told that you that it didn't matter what the Muslims wanted because the Serbs didn't want Muslims living in Pale. And I'd like to ask you, just to be clear, Was Malko Koroman also present when Mr. Koljevic said this to you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Even before that meeting was organised, we asked Malko Koroman and the president of Pale municipality to guarantee our safety so we don't have to move out. But they kept sending us back and forth. And then we went to the chief of the police and asked him to bring someone from the authorities for a meeting so we can take to them directly. And a meeting was set up in a private tavern. We came there. Malko was present. And just for a while, one of the policemen, Predrag Jovicic, disappeared for about ten minutes. And then he came back, bringing Nikola Koljevic. And we chatted. And then I asked, Is there a way, any way for us to find a way to live together as we had lived so far, to defuse these tensions so we don't leave our homes? And Nikola Koljevic says in exactly these words; I can quote him by heart: There's little use in you wanting to live with Serbs in Pale because the Serbs don't want to live together with you. And we just eyed each other at that. And then Malko Koroman added that he could not keep under control the Red Berets that had arrived from Knin. They want to do their job, and he cannot guarantee our safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And can I just ask you, At that point, did you have any understanding or any idea of what the job of the Red Berets was, when Mr. Koroman said, They want to do their job?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to see on television what the Serbian television was showing, how in Knin and Gospic they were referring to the Red Berets capturing Knin and Gospic. But they were practically burned to the ground. People were killed, wounded, looted, especially in Gospic. The whole small town was up in flames. And we thought, since he said that they, the Red Berets, had come from Knin and that they were billeted at the Panorama Hotel that they could do the same thing to the non-Serb population in Pale as they did in Knin and Gospic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Koroman say whether any measures would be taken to protect you from the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat it. He said that he couldn't keep them under control for long and that he couldn't guarantee our safety from the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on. In Krajisnik you also described being visited by two policemen, Jovan Skobo and another named Stanar who tried to convince you to leave Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And this is at transcript page 5322 in Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, who were they speaking to? Were they coming to speak to you alone as an individual, or were they speaking to groups of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Not with me in particular. At the time, there was a lot of fear for us. As soon as a police car would appear, we would be thinking that they were coming to intervene for some reason. And people would spontaneously begin to approach the car one by one asking, Why did you come? And then, since a lot of people gathered around, they said, You need to move out; you will have to move out. We said, Why? For what reason? What did we do wrong? And then Jovan Skobo said, like this: It's better for you to move out, rather than to have us hunt you down in the woods and catch you and drive you out. So we didn't know what to do. We didn't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And when you talk about approaching a car, are you saying this is a car containing Jovan Skobo and this Mr. Stanar?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, I'm thinking of that car, the police car.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, we touched briefly on -- sorry, in your Krajisnik testimony, you touched on the arming of Serbs. With the Serbs in Pale being armed, did you ever have any problems with these weapons being used in a way that caused you, as Muslims, any fear?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. Problems began before 1992, as far as the arming is concerned. Ten days before the new year, they began; before the new year of 1992. Suddenly you could hear loud shooting around the urban part of Pale. And we thought, Well, it's new year's eve. They're celebrating before the new year. It will pass. The new year eve celebrations came and went, but the shooting didn't stop. And then on the Serbian Orthodox Christmas, January 7th, we hoped that it would stop. But then the Orthodox Christmas came and went and the shooting didn't stop. There was increasing psychological pressure because of the shooting. It didn't stop, day and night. And this wasn't in the centre of town but it was a little bit outside of the centre. You could hear shooting from automatic weapons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you know someone by the name of Bekto Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I know him very well. He's a barber, and his house was shot at from automatic weapons and also hand-grenades were thrown at his house. It was probably one of the neighbours. His brother was probably killed in some action, when the Serbs went into action, and it was done out of revenge, as far as that could be revenged. The house was attacked in this way. The windows and the facade were damaged by the hand-grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: What ethnicity was Bekto Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: As far as you were aware, did the police take any action to stop this random shooting that was going on around the town?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I don't have the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'll ask that question again. Sorry, that wasn't translated, Mr. Crncalo. As far as you are aware, did the police take any action to stop all the shooting that was going on around Pale town?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No action was taken. We asked at those meetings -- we asked Malko Koroman, and he would reply saying that in the -- using the Bosnian word, that they were just "senluciti," just celebrating and going a bit wild, as celebration, and that that would pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now you've described your own arrest. Are you aware of any other Muslims being arrested around Pale during this time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. I can say their names: Hrvo, Fehim was arrested; Izet Jasarevic; Nasko Smaic; Alija Jusufovic; none of them came out of prison. They were all killed in prison. There were random arrests on the street. I was watching. It was all young people. Those two who would take people by their arms and take them to the car and take them to the police station are unknown to me. And the person who was pointing out who would be arrested on the street was a man named Zoran Skobo; he was a professor at the technical engineering school in the Pale municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now I'd like to just ask you a couple of questions to clarify what you've just said. These individuals that you named who were arrested, Izet Jasarevic and others, you said none of them came out of prison. What was the prison that they were taken to?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: They took them to the police. That was when the prison was set up. Every police station has some room or a cell where they can place perpetrators, but this one was actually set up in the old cinema hall where films used to be shown, earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And who arrested them and took them to the cinema hall?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, the police. Who else?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, are you also aware of an incident where some paramilitaries took some gold from a woman and she complained to the police?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I don't know her name, but I know her husband's name is Agan Kadiric. They confiscated jewelry from his wife, all that she had, and they went and complained to the police. But then it was returned to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Was she Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, Muslim. She was a Muslim woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So in this case, the police were able to get this gold back after being taken by the paramilitaries. Are you aware of any action being taken against paramilitaries in Pale by the police for any of the more serious crimes they committed against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: When you say you don't know about that, do you mean you don't know whether any action was taken; or no, there was no action taken against them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I don't think that they did take any action. I mean, that would be something that would be known, had they initiated any steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: With the -- the paramilitaries in Pale town, are you able to estimate the number that were present in Pale through this period?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: There was a barracks, Jahorinski Potok, in Pale, and it's a large barracks in size. But it never had a lot of soldiers there. But now, what you're asking me about, I really couldn't be sure. But there were thousands of them, paramilitaries, the regular real army should have been in the barracks together with its weapons. That's where they were. But the others were wandering around Pale armed, and there were too many of them. But I really couldn't say whether there were 10, 15 of them. I mean, I really don't dare. But there were thousands of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So, in your view, would it have been possible for these paramilitaries to have gone around unnoticed in Pale town?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No, it wasn't possible for them to move around unnoticed. They didn't hide themselves either. They were shirtless. They had these ribbons around their foreheads, their arms. They had knives, guns at their waists. They were driving around in open vehicles. They didn't even try to hide. They wanted to show themselves, almost.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on now to something else you talked about in Krajisnik. And this was some Muslim men who were brought to Pale town from Bratunac. And you described an incident in May 1992, when three truck-loads of Muslim men from Bratunac were brought into Pale. And you said that the truck stopped near the police station, and you could see that the men had fresh wounds and blood on their faces. I'd like to ask you, While these trucks were stopped there, did you see any police in the area?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: When the trucks stopped, I just was passing by there by chance. And I'm not glad I saw that today. Well, anyway, when they stopped, the police came out to see what was going on. And when they saw the people in the vehicles, people were saying, Here are some Balijas that were caught in Bratunac. And they added that it was the Green Berets. But none of the men had a cap on their head of any kind, and they had those rubber miner's boots, the ones that go up to the knees. They had work pants. Some of them were wearing work shirts; some didn't, some shirt [as interpreted]. But it was all clothing that was dirty from soil or from being in the stables, from excrement. You could see that these people were rounded up from some type of agricultural farming tasks and rounded up and brought in these vehicles. And then I don't know; perhaps it was the head of the municipality, Starcevic, who started to shout at these people, that they had brought them. Why are you bringing them here to me? I have no place for them. And then used these very words: Take them back to where you got them from. Everyone was silent. I didn't wanted to stay around for much longer. I heard later that they had been accommodated in the cinema hall next to the police station. I call it a prison, and it was, a war time prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'll move on to another topic. Did you know someone by the name of Fehim Hrvo.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, that was my neighbour. He was taken to prison, and he didn't come out of the prison alive. He was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: When you say he was taken to the prison, which building are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: The cinema hall. The old cinema hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, how did you find out that Mr. Hrvo had died?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: A police patrol came to the street, and they were looking for volunteers to go to prison to bring out a dead body from the prison. They came to our street looking for people who dared to go and take out a dead body from the prison. I didn't go. Some others did. And they picked up the body and brought it back to our street. And we buried him that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: When this police patrol came to the street looking for volunteers, did they say how Mr. Hrvo had died?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: They did mention it. They said that he had hanged himself. But there were no markings whatsoever on his neck that you could tell by -- that the man had been hanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So you say he didn't have any markings around his neck. Did he have any sort of markings or injuries on his body or his head or face?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No. We didn't really uncover the body to take a good look. When he was brought back, there was an escort, a police escort, about ten policemen who came. They all had automatic rifles. I will never erase that image from my head. And instead of them being civil, because there was a dead man there, they were holding their guns at the ready and pointed them at us and at this dead body, when we were taking the body down from some trailer, to take it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the police conducted any investigation into Mr. Hrvo's death?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I don't know. But I don't think that they did, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Earlier on you mentioned some other people who had died whilst in custody. Amongst them was Izet Jasarevic and some others. Do you know if there was any police investigation into their deaths?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: There was no investigation. Izet Jasarevic, Alija Jusufovic, and Nasko Smaic; they were also killed in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on now to another topic, and this is the transfer of your property. You testified in Krajisnik about having to sign over your property to a Serbian woman. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could we call up 65 ter 2463.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, you'll see a document coming up on the screen before you. Mr. Crncalo, we have a technical problem with the B/C/S version of this document, so I have a hard copy here, which I'll ask the usher to perhaps hand to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I -- I'm sorry, I'm sorry, Your Honours. If I may be of assistance. We uploaded the very same document also, as Defence Exhibit 1D03-4102. I'm sorry, I'm sorry. I thought it was the missing -- the Serbian document; that's why I stood up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, is this the contract that you signed, exchanging your property? I know it's difficult to read. But can you recognise that as the contract for exchange of property?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And do you recognise your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now I'd just like to look at the item number IV where it states that the exchange is to be temporary until the war ends. Did you, in fact, get your property back at any time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I did get my house back in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry, in the transcript it says that you got your house back in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I handed it over in 1992. In 2002, I got it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And how did you go about getting it back?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: There were these international organisations in Sarajevo that dealt with the property matters, because after the Dayton Accords, no one felt comfortable to go back to the municipalities from which people were expelled. There was this international organisation, CRPC, that was dealing with the submission of requests and the restoration of property. They would check whether the requests for restoration of property were authentic; and, if they were, then those organisations helped the people to get their property back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, at the time that you exchanged your property or you signed this document handing your property over, what, if anything, were you allowed to take from your home?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: We were allowed to take only -- we could take stuff in our hands. I had a car. And it was not only me, but none of the citizens of Pale were permitted to take their passenger or freight vehicle with them. We could take with us only what we could pack and take in our hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd seek to tender this document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1463, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if I could now call up 65 ter 2465.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, another document will be coming up on screen in front of you in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if we could please go to page two of the English, remaining on page 1 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, this is an excerpt from a register of contracts for the exchange of properties. And if you look down at the bottom on the B/C/S page, can you see an entry for the transfer of your house to a woman named Dragica Subotic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And is that your signature next to that entry?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you sign this document at the police station in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: This was signed at the municipal office, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1464.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd now like to call up 65 ter 2460.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: This, Mr. Crncalo, is a decision of the Serbian Municipality of Pale on the change of residence of Muslim and Croatian citizens. And you will see at the bottom that it's signed by the president, Radoslav Starcevic. First of all, I will ask you: Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If we look at Article 1, it states there that: "Citizens of Muslim and Croatian ethnicity who wish to change their residence can exercise that right with the agreement of and permission from the Pale Public Security Station." Now, is this consistent with what you experienced, that, when you were approached to exchange your property, it had to be done through the police?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: It worked this way. People who had not signed any contract with anyone - and I did - had to go to the police and turn in the keys of their homes. And I said a moment ago, anyone who did not leave Pale during the war did not survive. If you look at it realistically, and we all made that decision, it's better to save the lives of your family than your property. So we sacrificed our property to save our lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And when you signed the exchange of your property, this had to be done with the permission of the police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the police. The police made provision for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: He has never seen it before and doesn't know about it, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I understand he hasn't seen it before, Your Honour. In my submission, it's a document that's regular on its face. I don't know if there's any specific challenge to its authenticity. It's certainly relevant to his testimony, and he's able to talk about the content of it, the involvement of police in the exchange of properties. And it certainly corroborates his version of what happened when he was forced to sign over his property.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I -- I -- Your Honours, I don't have the objection of -- of admittance of this document. But I have a problem with the misinterpretation of the document which -- which Mr. Dobbyn is constantly repeating. Because this has nothing to do with the -- with the change of property. This is concerning the change of the -- of the -- of the -- what is the -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The change of residence. This is -- this document concerns the change of residence. And it says, For the persons of Muslim and Croatian nationality, or ethnicity, who want to change their residence. So voluntary, they want to change their residence, they can. That is what this document says. It has nothing to do with the property whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, be that as it may, Mr. Crncalo changed his residence. That had to be done through the police. That's exactly what he's testified to, and this is what this document shows also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly what I -- what I was -- what I was objecting about, because he didn't testify about that. He said that he went to the municipal building and signed the contract on exchange of property. It has nothing do with the police whatsoever. But Mr. Dobbyn insisted on that for a couple of times and is mixed and is confusing the witness about the change of residence and the change of property, because those are two completely different issues and things. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you have -- no, you indicated that you had no objection to the application of admission of the document by itself --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that is correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... in other words, there is no -- do I take it that you do not take issue with the position of the Prosecution that it is a regular document? The effect and intent is a different thing which would be a matter of argument later down. But you have no difficulty with the basic regularity of the document as an official document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We do not contest that this is an official document. At least it appears; I cannot, of course, guarantee that. But I understand the reluctance of the Trial Chamber because of admitting this document with this witness. But -- because the witness had never seen it or has anything to do with. So the nexus, I understand, is missing. But, still, I wanted to say to the Trial Chamber that we do not object on admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, actually, for myself, I've gone past the nexus. I was just looking at the regularity of the document as an official document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In the context of that document being out there, Mr. Dobbyn is making an argument which you are vigorously resisting. I see that. But that's all a matter, at the end of the exercise, for submissions by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honours. And, again, we do not object to -- to the authenticity of the -- of this document and its relevance, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, it -- it appears that this document may be useful to you at some point. But where we are now in terms of what this witness has testified, we -- we don't propose to accede to your application to admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, I'm going to move now to the issue of the bus convoys from Pale and, in particular, the bus convoy that you were a part of that left Pale. And in your prior testimony, in Krajisnik, you described the convoys that transported non-Serbs out of Pale town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, just for the record, this is at transcript page 5348. Where this starts in the Krajisnik testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And in relation to that, you said, in Krajisnik, that they rounded up all the people, and they were taken away. When you said "They rounded up all the people," who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: You mean took them away in convoys? Is that the question you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: What I'm asking is, Who rounded up the people and put them on these convoys?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: If the police was escorting us all the way from getting onto the bus until we got onto the bus, then, of course, it was the police. Who else could it be? And they did escort us all the way. So it was the police who did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: You mentioned a while back that you -- you owned a car. Was leaving Pale in your own car -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I did. I did have a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And was leaving Pale in your own car an option that was available to you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: It was not possible for me or anyone who lived in the urban area of Pale to take their car when leaving, when moving out. There were people who had more than one car, including freight vehicles. There were people who were professional hauliers in Pale, many of them. But the police did not allow cars to be used. You could carry only what you could carry in a bag or in your hands. And I also have to say, about these swaps: People are trying to insinuate here that I voluntarily left, voluntarily swapped my property. People, who would possibly make a blind swap, not knowing what you're getting in return? Is there a person who would do such a thing voluntarily? When I came to the address I was given, half of the house was destroyed. That was the swap I got.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, do you expect to finish with this witness before the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If -- I have about another 15 minutes, Your Honours. Should we continue after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We've been alert that the OTP, in the person of Mr. Hannis, wishes to raise a matter before the witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it has to do with scheduling. Witness ST-119 was the witness who was scheduled for a videolink. We cancelled that on Friday, after talking with him. His health had gotten worse, his memory was worse. We made a decision not to call him. We have found a witness who was able to come, travel today, to testify later this week. It's ST-160, I believe. However, he's just arrived; I think his plane touched down within the past half-hour or so. He is expected to be here about 2.00 to begin proofing. The Stanisic Defence has requested to meet with whim, and that's tentatively scheduled for 4.00. We would like to consult with the witness this afternoon and see if he feels comfortable in starting tomorrow, as soon as this witness is finished, whether that's at 9.00 or sometime later. But we wanted to alert you to the possibility that, if he says, I just got here; I need a little more time, and maybe a delayed start for him tomorrow as well. I just wanted to bring that to your attention. And we will advise the parties and Your Honours as soon as we found out. And I wanted to make an anticipatory request for a delayed start in case that is indeed what happens. The following witness for later this week is ST-168. I have two hours for direct examine; I think the Defence has requested four and a half total. So I still think, even if there is a delayed start tomorrow, for the next witness, we will finish this week without any problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In terms of tomorrow, as presently advised, what is the latest you think you would wish to begin?

utterances.speaker: MR.  HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Di Fazio will be leading the witness. I haven't had a chance to speak with him. It might be like today. We might request to start at 11.00. It's beginning to look now as though the current witness may spill over partly into tomorrow, so it may not be as big a gap as I first anticipated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll see. [Microphone not activated] ... if the witness who is -- who is not -- if the witness does, in fact, finish tomorrow, the Registry needs to be in a position to know by this afternoon whether, in fact, we would be starting late tomorrow. So the -- we will see how the rest of the day goes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HANNIS
utterances.text: We will advise you as soon as we can, to avoid any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Hello again, Mr. Crncalo. We'll carry on from where we left off before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And I would like to show Exhibit P1453.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Crncalo, what you see in front of you is a proposal from the Muslim community that was sent to the Pale Crisis Staff. It was concerning arrests of unarmed members of the Muslim community. Now, the first paragraph, point -- sorry, the first paragraph, not numbered, refers to a meeting held by a group of Muslim citizens from Pale on the 9th of April, 1992. Now, were you involved in any such meetings of concerned Muslim residents of Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. Several times I participated in such meetings, asking for a possibility to be given to us to stay in Pale and to live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if we look at this particular document, we can see that among the proposals that were put forward were joint patrols; we see removal of barricades; and presence of all ethnicities and all contacts between -- in the municipality. Now, we see that this was sent to the Crisis Staff apparently. In the proposal also, if you look at number 4, it asks that: "Representatives of the Muslims and other citizens be co-opted into the Pale municipal Crisis Staff." Now, as far as you are aware, were there any non-Serb members of the Crisis Staff in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Are you aware whether any one particular political party dominated the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, the Crisis Staff was set up by the SDS party in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd now like to move on and show Exhibit P1454.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, you can see that this is the Crisis Staff's response to the proposals of the 10th of April. Now, first of all, I would ask you if you ever saw this document yourself?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it the last time I testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If we could look at the first conclusion here, Mr. Crncalo. It states: "There is no reason for the Muslim population to panic and move out. The Serbian Municipality of Pale shall offer full protection to all citizens of Pale municipality, whatever their ethnicity or creed." And, Mr. Crncalo, in your experience, was this undertaking to protect all citizens in Pale followed through?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I gave this account several times, and I'll do it again: We asked for safety and the possibility to go on co-existing in Pale. But the last time we made that request, the answers from Koljevic and Koroman meant that we had to move out, that our safety cannot be guaranteed. And Malko Koroman said he could not protect us from the Red Berets, so we felt no guarantee of safety was given by the municipality authorities in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Moving on to the second conclusion there. It states that: "Supplies will be provided equally to all parts of the municipality." And, Mr. Crncalo, did all groups in the municipality receive equal supplies during after time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: That time - and I will limit myself to the period in 1992 until the 2nd of July when I left - what you could find in the shops, in the area where I lived, was the barest minimum. And in Korane, they had a sign in the shop windows that there are no goods to be sold for no Serbs [as interpreted]. It's the local community of Korane.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd just like to clear that up. Korane, is -- was that a Muslim or Serb area?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: It was mixed. Majority Serb, as in the whole of Pale. In the local commune of Korane, there were Muslims, but they were less than 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: The answer you gave earlier has been translated as: "... they had a sign in the shop windows that there are no goods to be sold for no Serbs." I'd just like to get some clarification on that. Are you saying that goods would be sold to non-Serbs or would not be sold to non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Goods will not be sold to non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, going back to this document from the Crisis Staff, the third conclusion is a proposal that: "Issues be agreed on by an inter-party commission composed of members of the Pale SDS and SDA." Are you aware of the existence of any such commission?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I was not a member of the SDA party, although I was a follower. As far as that committee is concerned, or commission, the population would have been aware of its work. And I can say with certainty that there was no such commission among the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on now to another issue that you touched on in your Krajisnik testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we do so.

utterances.speaker: MR.  DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, I'd like to ask the witness how he perceived this apparent contradiction between the two indications, given, on the one hand by the Crisis Staff, as we see here on the screen, that there's no reason for the Muslim population to panic and to move and so on and so forth; and, on the other hand, the televised messages given by Koroman and others at the time that Muslims should leave as soon as they could. How did you perceive these two contradictory messages, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document that I saw, the last time I testified and today, I had never been aware of it before I came here, and I did not know that such a thing was written and put on some sort of agenda at the meetings of the Pale municipality. On the other hand is something entirely different that I lived through, and that's the same experience other people like me had: and that was daily pressure, ranging from shooting in the air to arrests of certain persons who were later carried out dead, out of the prison, and the rounding up of young men in the streets. I think I was quite clear. I saw this document for the first time here, and I can understand what you say about my testimony and this document being in contradiction. But I'm seeing this document -- in fact, I saw this document for the first time last time I came here to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. 33, line 6, I believe the witness's answer is part of your question, so just for the sake of the clarity of the transcript, this should be remedied. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that that is actually my question there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: To move on and to follow up on His Honour Judge Harhoff's question, you've said that you weren't aware of this document before having come to the Tribunal the last time to testify. Were there any sort of public notices or pronouncements in Pale during the first half of 1992, encouraging Muslims to stay put and that they were safe there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Announcements or proclamations or good news that we could stay to live in Pale did not exist, at least until I was living there, the 2nd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on now to something you touched on in your prior testimony, and that's -- you mention an occasion when Radovan Karadzic was in Pale and gave a speech. Can you recall when this took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm really sorry. I have to object to this. Your Honours, this -- maybe the witness should remove his headphones. I don't know if he speaks English. Or maybe he could be excused until we clarify the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the witness should be excused for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm really sorry for disturbing the proceedings in this way, but I think this is important. The -- the 92 ter package which was offered by the Prosecutor is the -- his -- the testimony of the witness in Krajisnik case. In Krajisnik case, during the whole case or in all his previous testimonies, he never, ever mentioned this episode with Mr. Karadzic. This episode only appeared in the transcript in his testimony at Karadzic in April 2010. Now, based on that, I don't -- I don't really see the basis for this question by -- by my learned friend, Mr. Dobbyn. Because if the -- if the Prosecution wanted this on the record or as an issue in -- in this case, they -- they could have covered his transcript -- his testimony, his transcript of his testimony in Karadzic. Now, they opted for Krajisnik. I'm -- I mean, I really have a problem with that. If it's a 92 ter package and it's a 92 ter witness, that they -- that they go beyond -- that the -- that the Office of the Prosecutor seeks to go beyond what is -- what is obviously a frame of the 92 ter testimony of the witness. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could reply to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, his 92 ter package and his summary from Krajisnik talks about persecution, increased public manifestations of nationalism, the conditions under which the non-Serb population was living. This issue that I'm about to address now certainly comes under that. So there is notice about this sort of thing. Furthermore, at the time that his 92 ter package was put together, he obviously hadn't testified in Karadzic. He testified in Karadzic in April of this year. However, that's been disclosed to the Defence. As we can tell from submissions, they are aware of that. This does build on the issues that are contained in his package, in his 65 ter summary. And, yes, we could have taken the approach of adding an additional transcript to his 92 ter package, but, really, for this one point, that really doesn't seem worthwhile. It would be burdening the Trial Chamber with a whole new transcript of another case, when there's this one point that we feel adds to what's in his summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Except, Mr. Dobbyn, that now that you are specifically relying on it, not having made the application to -- at the risk of, quote/unquote, burdening the Trial Chamber, isn't there a basis for Mr. Zecevic's objection, that until you proffered the question to the witness now, he would have had no indication that you sought to rely -- you sought to go beyond the existing 92 ter package and add material from the Karadzic trial in April of this year?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, in my submission, this certainly doesn't go beyond any of the topics that are contained in his 92 ter package, and it certainly comes squarely within what's contained in his 65 ter summary: the conditions that the non-Serbs were living in, the threats that were being made against them, the uncomfortable tension that was being caused by the various leaders in the area. And this is -- just certainly comes under that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I do have one point that I'd like to add, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: In my submission, Your Honour, that if there is a problem with this, then the way to address it is to be giving the Defence more time to prepare for cross-examination. Certainly, as I've said, it's contained within the bounds of the 65 ter summary, this type of incident. If they feel that they haven't had sufficient notice, the proper remedy is not to prevent us from putting this evidence forward to the Trial Chamber, but to give Defence more time to prepare for cross-examination to address this point, if that's what they need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, the -- this speech, Mr. Karadzic's speech, that event, is that specifically mentioned in the summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. This specific speech is not mentioned. As we say, those -- our 65 ter summaries and 92 ter package were put together well before he testified in Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may add one -- one -- one thing. This all could have been remedied by the contents of the proofing note. Now, the proving note is silent about this. This is a very specific incident, that Karadzic's speech, alleged speech, in Pale on certain occasion is a very specific incident which has been challenged and discussed at the -- at the Karadzic trial. So during the proofing of this witness, this wasn't -- or maybe it was discussed, but it wasn't -- we were not made aware of the fact that it was discussed. And that is why I -- I don't think that -- that -- that this is a proper way of conducting the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this isn't something that came up for the first time during proofing. It came up in the Karadzic case, and that testimony has been disclosed to Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow the question, but the remedy that we would apply is to permit the -- counsel for -- for the Accused Stanisic additional time to deal with this specific question. So that means that we'll take the witness into tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dobbyn, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, I'll just return to the question that I asked you before we took a short break. In your Krajisnik testimony, you mentioned an occasion when Radovan Karadzic was in Pale and gave a speech. Now, can you recall when this took place?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I think it was in the first half of July. I can't tell you the exact date. But it was in the first half of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Were you able to hear any of the speech that he gave?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I did not stay for long, but I did hear a bit. First, he was talking about the defusing of tensions that arose over the deaths of close family members of those present. And then he said, By attacking every Muslim house, you are protecting your own home. He did not specify where or whose house, but he just said, By attacking every Muslim house, you protect your own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Where did he give this speech?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Near the culture hall, which was, at the time, the seat of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Moving on, Mr. Crncalo, do you have any knowledge of any sort of attack on the village of Hrenovica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I do. The last time I came to testify, a document was shown to me in relation to the collection of weapons from Muslims. And the document clearly bears the title: "Military action in the territory of Hrenovica." I said then, and I say now, when you collect weapons, it was collected the way I described, when I and all the other people came to a certain place to hand over their weapons. Whereas, this was a military operation to capture territory. And, at the time, two policemen were killed, and perhaps four were wounded. After that, an order came out from Malko Koroman that all the weapons in the hands of Muslims should be turned over to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And just to be clear, is Hrenovica largely a Muslim settlement?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: It was not purely Muslim. The population was mixed, like in all the other parts of Pale. But the Muslims lived there in a higher percentage than Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And do you know if any civilians were killed in this attack?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I know that many civilians were arrested and brought to the prison in Pale. And there were some among them who were so badly beaten that they could not survive. They succumbed to their injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when this operation on Hrenovica took place?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Early May, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Earlier on you mentioned that two policemen were killed, or perhaps four. So is it your understanding that police were involved in this -- this operation?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Of course. How else would they get killed if they did not participate?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. And now the final matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd like to call up Exhibit P990.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And what you will see coming up before you, Mr. Crncalo, in a moment, is a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And is it possible to blow that up any -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, do you recognise what this photo -- photograph shows?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I can. This is the urban part of Pale municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, with the help of the usher, I wonder if you could mark the location of the police station.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Is this enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If you could just put a circle completely around the building, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And within that circle could you write the number 1.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in this photograph, can you locate the former cinema where you say a prison operated?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And could you mark that with the number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. You've also -- you -- referring to the speech that was given by Radovan Karadzic that was given outside the cultural building, can you find the cultural building and put a circle around that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if you could mark that with the number 3.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: One moment, I'm sorry, I haven't finished. You also described the incident where trucks filled with Muslim men from Bratunac arrived in Pale. Could you mark with an X the location where these trucks pulled up and stopped?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And just above those Xs, could you put the number 4.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, is the location where you were loaded onto buses in the convoy that left Pale on the 2nd of July, is that visible on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, no. We would need to look at the right side of the photograph, because you can't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all the marks I need on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask that this be given a new exhibit number and admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1465, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have a question to you, because you asked the witness just a while ago about three or four policemen killed in Pale. Now let me see if I can find it. The reason I wanted to get back to it was that your question was a bit ambiguous, because it sounded to me as if you are -- ah, here it is. It's on page 40, line 20. Can you get back to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And this is your question to the witness: "Earlier on you mentioned that two policemen were killed, or perhaps four. So is it your understanding that police were involved in this operation?" And the witness answered: "Of course. How else would they get killed if they didn't participate?" Who -- first of all, let me ask you if -- if this is a reference to Adjudicated Fact 1313 which reads that at least three Muslims were killed by Serb forces? I take it it's not the same incident, but I just wanted to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's not. And perhaps I could ask some further questions in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In any case, let -- let's get back to the -- my first part of the question, namely, the killing of two policemen. Of which ethnicity were those policemen? Were they Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: All right. So two Serbian policemen were killed, and Mr. Dobbyn's question to you was that they were killed because they took part in an operation. Do you recall what that operation was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was an attack on Hrenovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I have nothing further to add to that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Dobbyn. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Crncalo.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to start with a couple of questions about the context of your testimony in the Krajisnik case. In the Krajisnik case, on page 5.305 of the transcript, you said that, according to what you know, the mobilisation that was carried out in 1991 and 1992 did not include Muslims but affected only the Serbs who lived in the Pale municipality territory. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember that testimony very well, and I can tell you that I'm right for saying that. Look, when we spoke about the statement of Karadzic a couple of minutes ago, the Muslims, at the time, young men from my street, tried to go to the hospital to give blood for the wounded who were brought in by helicopter from Zepa. They were turned back. They didn't want to take their blood to help the wounded. Never mind mobilise a Muslim into the army. So I think I said what I said correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you to make a break, a slight pause, between my question and your answer, because what we say needs to be interpreted. Thank you. The fact is, sir, that, isn't it, that the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA, like all the officials of the -- of Muslim ethnicity in the Socialist Federal Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina appealed on ethnic Muslims not to respond to the JNA call-up. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I'm going to answer that question. Yes, that's how it was. But does anybody ask why?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a sufficient answer that this was really so. Sir, can you tell me, it's correct, isn't it, that already in early 1992 there were check-points on the Sarajevo-Pale road. Do you remember that? You also talked about that in your testimony in the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Sarajevo-Pale, there were check-points on that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the Lapisnica location.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Who manned that check-point? The Serbs did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Green Berets at the station in Sarajevo, the bus station in Sarajevo, checked the IDs of all the people in early 1992, all the people who were going east towards Pale? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: When the check-points were set up that we just talked about, it wasn't just me, but almost the entire population of the Pale municipality couldn't really go to Sarajevo because they were turned back. When we were still going to work, before we were dismissed from our jobs, these -- this check-points at Lapisnica checked all the IDs of the people entering Pale. Once we were fired, there was no longer any communication open at Korane. It was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please concentrate. I'm asking you about the early 1992 period, and you're talking about May 1992. Are you aware that the members of the Green Berets were checking the IDs of all the people at the bus station in Sarajevo, all the people who were going east towards Pale and Eastern Bosnia? Are I aware of this or not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Public Security Station Centar chief, a certain Ismet Dahic, already in late 1991 drove away all the Serb ethnic police officers from that public security station?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell me the Sarajevo-Centar municipality borders on the Pale municipality, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No, they don't border on each other. Their borders don't touch anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I made a mistake. It's not Centar, but Stari Grad municipality. The Stari Grad municipality and the Pale municipality are next to one another, they share a common border. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
