utterances.text: The Stari Grad and the Pale municipalities do have a common border.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since I made a mistake and I said that the public security station, Ismet Dahic was the chief in Stari Grad, are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Malko did mention another person as the chief in the Stari Grad Police Station. I think his name was Enes -- Enes, Eno. He would say, Eno, I need this or I need that. His name is Enes. He was the chief police officer. Malko never mentioned any Ismet Dahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this conversation was the one when Malko Koroman said that no police officer of Muslim ethnicity will be employed at the Pale station until a Serb ethnic policeman is employed at the Stari Grad-Sarajevo Police Station; is that the conversation we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. That is it when he mentioned Eno.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it correct that the Lapisnica check-point was set up on the road only after the Green Berets attacked the Serbian village in early April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I cannot understand that that would be the reason to set up the check-point. Because when people were still going to work, the check-point was already there, and people were living in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, from your testimony, we see that you went to work for the whole month of May. So I'm asking you about a particular moment in time when this check-point was set up in early April, after the attack by the Green Berets on this Serbian village, are you aware - yes or no - of this?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In March 1992, you were arrested -- or, rather, brought in to the public security station because you were on guard in front of your house with a rifle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: The rifle was leaning against the wall. That is true. But I was actually standing in front of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, this is a hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. It's a hunting rifle, a pump-action rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a licence for it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It was licensed at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you know very well, if you were registered for a weapon, if you had a licence, that in order to licence a hunting rifle, you had to be a member of some kind of hunters' society. That is what the rules are in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, before you could receive a licence for a weapon, you needed to be a member of some kind of hunters' association. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it's a fact, isn't it, that this hunting weapon that you had, this rifle, you were allowed to carry only when you went hunting. Isn't that right? That -- the licence didn't mean that you could walk around town with long-barrelled weapon?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, this is not a long-or a short-barrelled hunting weapon. This is a hunting rifle. There are no other ways to describe it. As for carrying weapons, you could carry it in town, but it would have to be in a holster. I didn't leave my yard. I was in my yard in front of my house. I wasn't carrying it anywhere or carrying it around anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the case in Sarajevo in 1995, before the investigative judge, you gave a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 1D03-4106.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You recall that on the 23rd of August, 1995, you did give a statement to the investigative judge in Sarajevo in the presence -- this was Judge Hadzic Ibrahim and Public Prosecutor Dzemila Begovic; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this is the first page. Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you had no reason not to tell the truth to the judge in Sarajevo in 1995.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I am a man of good character. I wouldn't tell an untruth to anyone on the street, never mind to any kind of official organ in any country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And before you began this testimony in 1995, you were warned about your duty to tell the truth, that you were not allowed to -- not to disclose anything, omit anything, and that you gave an oath that you would speak the truth?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I did give an oath here to speak the truth, and I did the same in Sarajevo as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So then there is no reason for us to doubt that the facts that are included in this statement are untruthful or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: It's up to you to believe this or that, and I'm here. So if something is not quite right, you can ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you say in the middle of the text somewhere, when you are describing this arrest on the 3rd and 4th of March - I don't know if you can see it - the sentence begins: "Thus, I was on the 3rd and 4th of March, 1992 ..." Would you like for us to zoom on that part of the document, where the numbers are? 0304.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can zoom in on the Serbian version please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it says there that you assert that on 3rd and 4th of March you were on guard duty in front of the house with a hunting rifle, when a vehicle arrived - I assume that it's a police vehicle - and that they picked you up immediately and took you to the police station. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is that what it says in the statement?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this is what happened?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, the car didn't actually come right in front of the house. They walked up to the house. They left the car a little bit before the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell me, In your testimony today, while this person called Hrsum, a police employee at the Pale Public Security Station, interrogated you that evening, you said that some other inspector came in in civilian clothing and that he forbade Hrsum from beating you anymore. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And he also said that he came from Sarajevo; he emphasised that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this inspector, he told you later -- you mentioned something about cigarettes. He told you that nobody was allowed to take your cigarettes from you. Is that what you told you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And he put them in my pocket himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Can you recall approximately at what time this inspector arrived?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I was beaten as much as I was beaten. So I think you need to understand me that I cannot really orient myself as to what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this was certainly before Malko Koroman came, because Malko Koroman found you in the corridor. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell approximately how much earlier this inspector in civilian clothing arrived before Malko Koroman arrived? If you can. If not, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I cannot. It was maybe two hours before. That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was two hours, then, before Malko Koroman came that this inspector in civilian clothing came and forbade Hrsum from beating you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I said two hours, but this is not certain. I was beaten. I was afraid. All I can do is just say something off the top of my head, but I'm not really sure whether that would be a correct estimate or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, after Malko Koroman came, this was after midnight, in any event?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He took you and your neighbour, who was also brought in, to this room and sat down to speak with you, and he threw this Hrsum person out; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, I was not brought in. I was arrested, and I had handcuffs on my hands. So don't try to paint it as something else. Second, the neighbour was still in there when Malko Koroman came. I was standing in the corridor by myself. And then Malko called me to this room and told Hrsum to leave the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I assert that you were not arrested because after this conversation with Malko Koroman you were released; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: And how would you treat it? When I had handcuffs on my hands? Was I arrested or not? I was handcuffed, firmly handcuffed. Well, you can define being brought in or being arrested with handcuffs on my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to enter into a discussion with you. These are legal terms, and I assume that you're not familiar with that. There is a difference. But this is not really that important. What's important are the facts. So can you please tell me, It's a fact that after that conversation that you had with Malko Koroman, Malko Koroman took you and your neighbour home in his own car. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And after March 1992, the situation deteriorated, the security situation in the Pale municipality; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this was a reflection of the situation in Sarajevo, first of all, which was really bad; the security situation, I mean?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I wasn't able to find out what was going on in Sarajevo. I am talking here about what I experienced on my own skin. This is where the reflection came from. I knew who implemented it, but I don't know where that came from. I cannot say one -- that one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the fact is, and you testified to that in your previous testimonies here at this Tribunal, that a large number of refugees, Serbs from Sarajevo, fled to Pale; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you saw them there, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The ones who came to my street to show themselves decked out with hand-grenades, automatic weapons with knives; those people, yes, I did see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you about refugees from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, they also showed themselves as being from Sarajevo, these refugees, and they joined up the army right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you're trying to tell me that they left their families in Sarajevo? Where were their women and children?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: They all came. They brought them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see their wives and children of those refugees from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, when I had to sign a contract that we talked about earlier, that is when I did see the mother of this Subotic, Miro; I saw her.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, would you kindly answer my questions? I'm asking you about the time in April and May. March, April, and May 1992. We will come to what you're talking about. This is July 1992. Can you please tell me if you saw Serb refugee families from Sarajevo in Pale during March, April, and May 1992? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Not during March. During April, I did. There was a person, a woman who came from Dobrinja; she came to my street; entered a house; and then complained to me at one occasion how little humanitarian aid she got, two or three kilos of potatoes and some margarine; and she was saying how was she going to survive on this for a week. I would see, also, the crush of unfamiliar people whenever cigarettes were being distributed. I did see that in Pale, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we've reached the point where we must take the adjournment for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir, I will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, we will resume tomorrow morning. And I must remind you that, having been sworn as a witness, you cannot have any communication with the lawyers from either side in the trial or -- and in such conversations as you have with persons outside the court, you cannot discuss your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
